title: Infra and Platform vs ML and Backend — persona playbook (quickplays)
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a compact, repeatable playbook for customer-facing reps and solution engineers to align messaging across three frequently-intersecting personas: ML Engineers (MLE), Backend Engineers, and Platform/Infra teams. Focus: concise talk tracks, primary objections and rebuttals, competitive callouts, and 30/60/90 enablement checklist for demos / POC framing.

Quick TL;DR for each persona (one liners):
- ML Engineers: "Give me consistent model outputs, fast iteration cycles, and easy evals so I can ship features without firefighting infra."
- Backend Engineers: "We need predictable latency and cost controls that behave under real traffic — drop-in API and sensible fallbacks."
- Platform/Infra: "We want a pluggable inference runtime we can operate at scale, audit, and integrate with our CD/observability stack."

Core themes to signal in every conversation:
- Production-first: SLOs, graceful degradation, and predictable unit economics.
- Observable & debuggable: per-route traces, token-level cost breakdowns, and eval hooks.
- Flexible deployment: hosted, dedicated, and private (VPC/on-prem) — same API and rollout controls across modes.

Persona-specific talk tracks and demo hooks
1) ML Engineers (MLE)
- Pain framing: "I iterate prompts, models, and evals constantly. Waiting on infra or noisy outputs slows feature velocity."
- Top value props: fast local dev loop (SDK + lightweight local runtime), built-in eval/regression alerts, model catalog with performance profiles, automatic caching to reduce cost without retraining.
- Demo hooks: show a prompt/regression test failing on first model, then show canary rollout to new model version with immediate quality metrics + automatic rollback on regression. Run a short eval set and show precision/recall/QA metrics over time.
- Proof points / talking data: highlight our snapshot of model A vs B across a 10k prompt set (latency median 45ms on dedicated, 3x lower token cost after prefix cache).
- Objections + rebuttals:
  * "I can run models locally or on Colab." -> "Local is good for experiments; production needs consistent infra. We give you a dev->staging->prod path with identical APIs and rolling model version control so your integration tests are meaningful."
  * "Model quality is what matters, not infra." -> "Totally — but model evaluation is only useful if you can test at scale and tie regressions to deploys. Our eval hooks link to rollouts and alert on metrics drift so you can ship faster with confidence."

2) Backend Engineers
- Pain framing: "We deploy features that must meet latency SLOs and predictable cost. Burstiness and noisy third-party APIs are a nightmare."
- Top value props: per-route latency SLOs and fallback policies, smart routing between cheaper quantized variants and high-quality variants, token-level billing visibility and per-route throttles.
- Demo hooks: show request routing in action: route 99% traffic to a quantized low-cost variant and 1% to a high-quality model for orthogonal checks; show failover to regional replica during simulated outage.
- Proof points: deterministic tail latencies (p99 stats) on Dedicated, cost per 1k tokens comparison against a baseline.
- Objections + rebuttals:
  * "Third-party APIs are simpler, we don't want another vendor." -> "We integrate like an API — but give you richer controls (routing, batching, cache) and observability. You get the same simplicity with far better operational safety."
  * "Latency is a deal-breaker." -> "We prioritize latency through kernel selection, batching configuration guidance, and edge-region placement. Show concrete p50/p95/p99 numbers on a similar app profile."

3) Platform / Infra / SRE
- Pain framing: "We need to operate inference safely at org scale: governance, cost predictability, and serviceability matter more than bells-and-whistles."
- Top value props: Private deployment option (VPC/on-prem) with the same control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, role-based access, and SLA-backed Dedicated pools. Rolling upgrades with canary/A-B and traceable rollout metadata.
- Demo hooks: open console, show RBAC, audit log example, and how a team pins a model version and applies an autoscaling policy. Show a simulated incident and how fallbacks/auto-scaling handled it.
- Proof points: enterprise customers on Dedicated with X% uptime, example SOC2/ISO controls we help meet.
- Objections + rebuttals:
  * "We need on-prem or air-gapped deployments; can you support our stack?" -> "Yes — we offer a private package and integrations with common KMS/HSM and observability systems. Customer-managed control plane option available for strict compliance needs."
  * "Don't want vendor lock-in." -> "We support open models and exportable model pinning; policies are config files and rollouts are reversible. We make exit easier than fully managed black boxes."

Competitive differentiation to call out (short notes)
- OpenAI/Hosted-first APIs: great for dev velocity. Callout: Redwood adds deterministic infra controls (routing, inexpensive variants, model lifecycle hooks) and transparent cost visibility at token level.
- Cloud endpoint products (SageMaker endpoints, Vertex AI): callout: these are infra primitives; Redwood layers opinionated runtime + smart routing + caching + evals and is faster to onboard for LLM-specific production needs.
- Self-hosted runtimes (LLM-serving OSS / vendor X): callout: more control but much higher ops cost; Redwood Dedicated + Private tries to strike the balance with operational tooling, autoscaling, and security integrations out of the box.
- Emerging inference startups: callout: compare on SLOs and fallbacks; ask for p99 proof and audit log granularity.

Language & framing guidance (dos and don'ts)
- Do: use concrete metrics (latency p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens) and tie to customer KPIs (checkout latency, recommendations throughput, ingestion budget).
- Do: translate infra features into developer velocity wins for MLEs and reliability wins for platform teams.
- Don't: overpromise model accuracy improvements or specific ROI without a quick POC to validate.
- Don't: use heavy vendor-speak — engineers want straight numbers and reproducible demos.

Suggested one-liners for different audiences
- For MLEs: "Ship models faster — same API from your notebook to prod, plus built-in regression guards so you don't wake up to broken prompts."
- For Backend: "Control latency and cost at route-level, with automated fallbacks and transparent token billing."
- For Platform: "Operate inference like any other platform service: RBAC, audit logs, CD integrations, and SLA-backed capacity."

30/60/90 enablement checklist (for AE/SE to run a technical POC)
- 0–30 days (Discovery + quick POC): capture traffic profile (qps, sequences, latency targets), agree on 5–10 eval prompts, spin up a small Dedicated demo or hosted sandbox, run baseline model and collect p95/p99.
- 30–60 days (Validate controls + scale): introduce routing policies, add canary rollout for model version, simulate region failover, validate billing reports and token breakdown. Integrate evals into CI.
- 60–90 days (Operationalize): configure autoscaling policies, deploy private option if required, hand off runbooks to platform, schedule training for SREs.

Open questions / work-in-progress (things to resolve before next enablement batch)
- We need templated PRs/playbooks for common verticals (search, summarization, chat) with demo data and expected baselines.
- Standardized p99 benchmarks for small/medium/large seq lengths and representative CPU/GPU hardware to use in field comps.
- POC pricing play — recommended discounts and usage caps for pilot customers (how we position cost vs value).

Suggested assets to attach to follow-up emails
- Short 2–3 slide one-pager: p95/p99 numbers + deployment options + recommended POC plan.
- A sample eval set (10–50 prompts) for the customer vertical.
- Link to our console quickstart video and a scripted demo checklist for SEs.

Notes to self / informal reminders
- Keep the talk tracks modular — mix and match for hybrid buyers (often one meeting has MLE + platform lead).
- Always ask: what is your p99 target? what failure modes are unacceptable? who is the escalation owner?
- Collect references from engineering customers who care about p99 and token cost transparency — these make the conversation concrete.

End of quickplay. Use this doc as a living working draft, update after 2 customer calls to capture new objections or proof points.
